claim: Two agents seated face-to-face engaged in game-theoretical tasks on a shared transparent touchscreen display.
source: We developed a setup where two agents seated face-to-face to engage in game-theoretical tasks on a shared transparent touchscreen display ('transparent games').
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental setup used in the study.

claim: Human and macaque pairs were compared in a transparent version of the coordination game 'Bach-or-Stravinsky'.
source: We compared human and macaque pairs in a transparent version of the coordination game 'Bach-or-Stravinsky', which entails a conflict about which of two individually-preferred opposing options to choose to achieve coordination.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the comparison made between species.

claim: Most human pairs developed coordinated behavior and adopted dynamic turn-taking to equalize payoffs.
source: Most human pairs developed coordinated behavior and adopted dynamic turn-taking to equalize the payoffs.
evidence: The manuscript reports the behavioral outcome observed in human pairs.

claim: All macaque pairs converged on simpler, static coordination.
source: All macaque pairs converged on simpler, static coordination.
evidence: The manuscript reports the behavioral outcome observed in macaque pairs.

claim: Two macaques learned to coordinate dynamically after training with a human confederate.
source: Remarkably, two animals learned to coordinate dynamically after training with a human confederate.
evidence: The manuscript describes the outcome of confederate training on macaque behavior.

claim: The confederate-trained macaque pair selected the faster agent's preferred option.
source: This pair selected the faster agent's preferred option, exhibiting turn-taking behavior that was captured by modeling the visibility of the partner's action before one's own movement.
evidence: The manuscript reports the specific coordination strategy observed in the confederate-trained pair.

claim: The turn-taking behavior in confederate-trained macaques was captured by modeling the visibility of the partner's action before one's own movement.
source: This pair selected the faster agent's preferred option, exhibiting turn-taking behavior that was captured by modeling the visibility of the partner's action before one's own movement.
evidence: The manuscript describes the modeling approach used to explain the observed behavior.

claim: The competitive turn-taking in macaques was unlike the prosocial turn-taking in humans.
source: Such competitive turn-taking was unlike the prosocial turn-taking in humans, who equally often initiated switches to and from their preferred option.
evidence: The manuscript compares the nature of turn-taking between species.

claim: Humans equally often initiated switches to and from their preferred option.
source: Such competitive turn-taking was unlike the prosocial turn-taking in humans, who equally often initiated switches to and from their preferred option.
evidence: The manuscript describes the switching behavior observed in humans.

claim: Dynamic coordination is not restricted to humans but can occur in rhesus monkeys with different social attitudes and cognitive capacities.
source: Thus, the dynamic coordination is not restricted to humans but can occur on the background of different social attitudes and cognitive capacities in rhesus monkeys.
evidence: The manuscript draws a conclusion about the generalizability of dynamic coordination across species.

claim: Action visibility promotes the emergence and maintenance of coordination when agents can observe and time their mutual actions.
source: Overall, our results illustrate how action visibility promotes the emergence and maintenance of coordination when agents can observe and time their mutual actions.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the main finding regarding the role of action visibility.

claim: The majority of primate species live in complex social groups with interactions ranging from intense competition to cooperation.
source: The majority of primate species live in complex social groups, in which interactions range from intense competition to cooperation (Byrne and Bates, 2010; Chang et al., 2013; Jaeggi et al., 2010; Joly et al., 2017; Platt et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature to support this general statement about primate social behavior.

claim: Individuals need to assess their own actions and goals, and those of other group members, while taking into account the history of interactions.
source: To adjust behavior optimally, individuals need to assess their own actions and goals, and those of other group members, while taking into account the history of interactions with and between these individuals (Frith and Frith, 2010; Platt et al., 2016; de Waal, 2007).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature to support this statement about social cognition requirements.

claim: Coordination is essential for maintaining cohesion between group members, avoiding conflicts, and achieving individual and joint action goals.
source: Coordination is essential for maintaining cohesion between group members, avoiding conflicts, and achieving individual and joint action goals.
evidence: The manuscript states the importance of coordination in social groups.

claim: Game theory offers a powerful framework to investigate dyadic social interactions.
source: Game theory, developed to study strategic interactions in rational decision-makers (Von Neumann and Morgenstern, 1944), offers a powerful framework to investigate dyadic social interactions (Rilling and Sanfey, 2011; Sanfey, 2007; Tremblay et al., 2017) and the evolution of coordination (Brosnan, 2018; Santos and Rosati, 2015; Smith, 1979).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature to support the use of game theory in studying social interactions.

claim: Humans, chimpanzees, rhesus macaques, and capuchin monkeys coordinate at above chance level on mutually beneficial high-reward/high-risk choices in the iterated Stag Hunt.
source: Humans (Homo sapiens), chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes), rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta), and capuchin monkeys (Cebus apella) coordinate at the above chance level on mutually beneficial high-reward/high-risk choices in the iterated Stag Hunt (Brosnan et al., 2012; Brosnan et al., 2011; Bullinger et al., 2011; Duguid et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature reporting coordination behavior across primate species.

claim: Humans often show a bias towards cooperative behavior in Prisoner's Dilemma.
source: Humans often show a bias towards cooperative behavior (Camerer, 2003; Rilling et al., 2002; Wedekind and Milinski, 1996).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature on human cooperative behavior in PD games.

claim: Macaques chose mutual cooperation significantly more and mutual defection significantly less than expected by chance in an iterated Prisoner's Dilemma game.
source: Remarkably, it was demonstrated that macaques, while mostly defecting, chose mutual cooperation significantly more and mutual defection significantly less than expected by chance, especially after preceding cooperation, in an iterated PD game (Haroush and Williams, 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites a specific study on macaque behavior in PD games.

claim: Humans, capuchins, and macaques often converge on anti-coordination in Conflict games.
source: Humans, capuchins, and macaques often converge on anti-coordination (Brosnan et al., 2017), but importantly, only humans alternate between the two individually-optimal anti-coordinated choices (Brosnan et al., 2017; Grueneisen and Tomasello, 2017; Helbing et al., 2005).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature on anti-coordination behavior across species.

claim: Only humans alternate between the two individually-optimal anti-coordinated choices in Conflict games.
source: Humans, capuchins, and macaques often converge on anti-coordination (Brosnan et al., 2017), but importantly, only humans alternate between the two individually-optimal anti-coordinated choices (Brosnan et al., 2017; Grueneisen and Tomasello, 2017; Helbing et al., 2005).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature showing species differences in alternating behavior.

claim: Alternating behavior in humans results in maximal and equal payoff for both agents and is called 'cooperative turn-taking'.
source: Such alternating behavior results in the maximal and equal payoff for both agents and is called 'cooperative turn-taking' (Bornstein et al., 1997; Colman and Browning, 2009; Noë, 2006).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature defining cooperative turn-taking.

claim: In Bach-or-Stravinsky game, each agent has an individually preferred option, but coordinating on either option adds the same bonus to both agents.
source: Each agent has an individually preferred option, but coordinating on either one of these options adds the same bonus to both agents.
evidence: The manuscript describes the payoff structure of the BoS game.

claim: In Bach-or-Stravinsky game, any coordinated choice is better than no coordination for both agents.
source: This renders any coordinated choice better than no coordination for both agents, but one coordinated choice is better for the first agent and the other better for the second agent.
evidence: The manuscript describes the payoff structure of the BoS game.

claim: Humans often take turns in Bach-or-Stravinsky games, switching between the two coordinated options to ensure fairness.
source: As in the Conflict game, games of the BoS type revealed that humans often take turns, switching between the two coordinated options to ensure fairness (Ioannou and Romero, 2014; Sonsino and Sirota, 2003).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature on human turn-taking behavior in BoS games.

claim: Trial-by-trial turn-taking frequently took place in 5-year-old children but neither in 3-year-old children nor in chimpanzees in a rope-pulling task.
source: Interestingly, in a rope-pulling task that requires cooperation but rewards only one agent at a time, trial-by-trial turn-taking frequently took place in 5-year-old children, but neither in 3-year-old children nor in chimpanzees (Melis et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study showing developmental and species differences in turn-taking.

claim: Real dyadic interactions often play out with the partner's actions in direct sight.
source: Yet, real dyadic interactions often play out with the partner's actions in direct sight (Dugatkin et al., 1992; van Doorn et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature on naturalistic dyadic interactions.

claim: The timing of one's own and the other's actions becomes part of the strategy space in transparent continuous time settings.
source: Thus, the timing of one's own and the other's actions becomes part of the strategy space (McDonald et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature on the role of timing in transparent games.

claim: A transparent continuous time setting can change choice strategies compared to classic simultaneous and sequential settings.
source: Such a 'transparent' continuous time setting can change choice strategies as compared to the classic simultaneous and sequential settings (Noë, 2006).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature on how transparency affects strategies.

claim: The concept of 'transparent games' extends classical evolutionary game-theoretic analysis to real-time interactions where visibility of partners' actions depends on relative action times.
source: To account for changes in strategies during action visibility compared to 'opaque' (simultaneous) choices, we recently developed the concept of 'transparent games' that extends the classical evolutionary game-theoretic analysis to real-time interactions in which the visibility of partners' actions depends on their relative action times (Unakafov et al., 2020; Unakafov et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript describes the theoretical framework developed by the authors.

claim: A novel dyadic interaction platform was designed where two agents face each other and act on the same visual objects on a vertical touch-sensitive transparent display.
source: To this end, we designed a novel dyadic interaction platform where two human or monkey agents face each other and act on the same visual objects on a vertical touch-sensitive transparent display between them.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental setup developed for the study.

claim: The transparent display configuration allows agents to monitor and react to each other's actions in real-time.
source: This configuration provides action visibility, i.e. it allows agents to monitor and react to each other's actions in real-time, emulating naturalistic interactions under well-controlled laboratory conditions.
evidence: The manuscript describes the capabilities of the experimental setup.

claim: Human or macaque agents were paired without explicit task instructions to facilitate inter-species comparability.
source: To facilitate inter-species comparability, we paired human or macaque agents without explicit task instructions.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental design choice.

claim: Transparency and instantaneous coaction were expected to facilitate efficient coordination in both species.
source: We expected that the transparency and instantaneous coaction (van Doorn et al., 2014) would facilitate efficient coordination in both species.
evidence: The manuscript states the authors' hypothesis about the effect of transparency.

claim: Humans were predicted to engage in pro-social turn-taking based on their cognitive abilities, propensity for fairness, and perspective-taking.
source: Based on their cognitive abilities (Proto et al., 2019), propensity for fairness (Peysakhovich et al., 2014), and perspective-taking (Devaine et al., 2017; Herrmann et al., 2007), we predicted humans to engage in pro-social turn-taking, where the reward maximization is alternated between partners.
evidence: The manuscript states the authors' hypothesis about human behavior with supporting citations.

claim: Macaques were predicted to utilize information about the partner's actions but be less likely to grant an advantage to the other player.
source: We predicted that macaques would also utilize the information about the partner's actions, but would be less likely to grant an advantage to the other player.
evidence: The manuscript states the authors' hypothesis about macaque behavior.

claim: Macaques were expected to coordinate to increase individual and joint rewards without turn-taking to balance rewards between players.
source: Instead, we expected that the monkeys would coordinate to increase individual (and joint) rewards, but without turn-taking to balance rewards between players.
evidence: The manuscript states the authors' hypothesis about macaque coordination strategy.

claim: Prior to the first dyadic session, each agent was individually trained to associate one color target with a larger reward.
source: Prior to the first dyadic session, each human or macaque agent in a pair was individually trained to associate one of the two color targets with a larger reward, so that the two agents preferred different colors.
evidence: The manuscript describes the training procedure used in the study.

claim: In dyadic trials, selecting the same target resulted in an additional reward on top of individually trained values.
source: In the dyadic trials, selecting the same target resulted in an additional reward on top of the individually trained values - such that choosing the same target was always better than choosing different targets, for both agents individually, and as a group.
evidence: The manuscript describes the payoff structure in dyadic trials.

claim: In coordinated trials, the agent whose individually preferred color was selected receives a larger reward.
source: But in such coordinated trials, the agent whose individually preferred ('own') color was selected receives a larger reward.
evidence: The manuscript describes the payoff structure in coordinated trials.

claim: The paradigm probes the ability to coordinate to obtain higher rewards and the capacity to deal with unfairness.
source: This paradigm probes the ability to coordinate in order to obtain higher rewards, and the capacity to deal with the unfairness introduced in each coordinated trial.
evidence: The manuscript describes the purpose of the experimental paradigm.

claim: 53% of human pairs (10 of 19) had balanced FCO values close to 0.5 for both agents, indicating alternating between colors using trial-by-trial or block-wise turn-taking.
source: The FCOs of 53% (10 of 19 pairs, teal underlay) had balanced values close to 0.5 for both agents, indicating alternating between colors, using either trial-by-trial or block-wise turn-taking.
evidence: The manuscript reports the proportion of human pairs showing turn-taking behavior.

claim: 47% of human pairs (9 of 19) had FCO of at least one agent close to one or zero, indicating fixed color selection.
source: The remaining 47% (9 of 19 pairs) had FCO of at least one agent close to one or to zero (both cases indicate a fixed color selection).
evidence: The manuscript reports the proportion of human pairs showing fixed color strategies.

claim: Five human pairs coordinated on a fixed color favoring one agent.
source: Five pairs coordinated on a fixed color favoring one agent (blue underlay).
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of pairs using this strategy.

claim: In two human pairs, both agents selected only their own preferred color.
source: Of the four pairs that did not coordinate successfully, in two pairs both agents selected only their own preferred color (red underlay).
evidence: The manuscript reports the behavior of pairs that did not coordinate.

claim: Most subjects from turn-taking dyads (17/20, 85%) realized the coordination benefit, compared to only half of non-turn-takers (9/18, 50%).
source: Based on the debriefing responses (Appendix 1, Supplementary file 5), most subjects from the turn-taking dyads (17/20, 85%) realized the coordination benefit, as compared to only half of non-turn-takers (9/18, 50%; Fisher's exact test p=0.035).
evidence: The manuscript reports debriefing results with statistical comparison.

claim: 14 of 20 turn-takers (70%) understood the payoff structure, compared to only 1 of 18 non-turn-takers (6%).
source: In addition, 14 of 20 turn-takers (70%) understood the payoff structure, compared to only 1 of 18 non-turn-takers (6%; Fisher's exact test p=0.00005).
evidence: The manuscript reports debriefing results with statistical comparison.

claim: All but five human pairs and all monkey pairs achieved an average joint reward >3.
source: All but five human pairs and all monkey pairs achieved an average joint reward >3 (no significant difference between species, Wilcoxon rank sum test: human dyads median 3.44, N 14; macaque dyads median 3.29, N 9; rank sum 192.5; p=0.297).
evidence: The manuscript reports the average joint reward with statistical comparison, and Figure 2C shows this data.

claim: Ten turn-taking human pairs showed a significant DCR with amplitude >0.2.
source: Ten turn-taking human pairs showed a significant DCR with amplitude >0.2 (teal dots, corresponding to the teal underlay in A, see also Figure 2—figure supplement 2C) while no monkey pair showed high DCR (only one pair showed a small (<0.2) but significant DCR, see also Figure 2—figure supplement 2H).
evidence: The manuscript reports DCR values for human pairs, and Figure 2D shows this data.

claim: No macaque pair showed high DCR; only one pair showed a small but significant DCR.
source: Ten turn-taking human pairs showed a significant DCR with amplitude >0.2 (teal dots, corresponding to the teal underlay in A, see also Figure 2—figure supplement 2C) while no monkey pair showed high DCR (only one pair showed a small (<0.2) but significant DCR, see also Figure 2—figure supplement 2H).
evidence: The manuscript reports DCR values for macaque pairs, and Figure 2D shows this data.

claim: Over all human pairs, there was a significant increase in median reward from early to late trials.
source: Over all pairs, there was a significant increase in median reward from early to late trials (Wilcoxon signed rank test: N 19, first 100 trials median 2.83, last 200 trials median 3.39, signed rank 12, p<0.0011, median change 0.56).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of reward changes over time in humans.

claim: All six macaques developed a strong preference for the target associated with the large reward in solo sessions.
source: All six macaques developed a strong preference for the target associated with the large reward (range 78–100%, mean 95% large reward color selection in the last solo session), before being paired with a conspecific with the opposite target color preference.
evidence: The manuscript reports the training outcome for macaques.

claim: In late dyadic sessions, all macaque pairs converged on coordination, either by converging on the same color target or on the same side.
source: In the late dyadic sessions, all pairs converged on coordination, in one of two distinct ways: either by converging on the same color target (Figure 2B, blue underlay, five pairs) or on the same side (green underlay, four pairs).
evidence: The manuscript reports the coordination strategies in macaque pairs, and Figure 2B shows this data.

claim: Across all macaque pairs, the average joint reward increased from early to late sessions (median early 2.75 versus late 3.29).
source: Across all pairs, the average joint reward increased from early to late sessions (median early 2.75 versus late 3.29; p<0.004, two-sided Wilcoxon signed rank test), and in 8 of 9 pairs, the proportion of coordinated trials increased significantly (p<0.05 Bonferroni corrected, Fisher's exact test; Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of reward changes over sessions in macaques.

claim: In 8 of 9 macaque pairs, the proportion of coordinated trials increased significantly from early to late sessions.
source: Across all pairs, the average joint reward increased from early to late sessions (median early 2.75 versus late 3.29; p<0.004, two-sided Wilcoxon signed rank test), and in 8 of 9 pairs, the proportion of coordinated trials increased significantly (p<0.05 Bonferroni corrected, Fisher's exact test; Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of coordination changes in macaques.

claim: High DCR values in humans coincided with non-zero values of both MI side and MI color.
source: Comparing the DCR and the MI measures revealed that high DCR values coincided with non-zero values of both MI side and MI color, indicating that dynamic coordination corresponds to both correlated side and correlated color choices between the agents (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D and E).
evidence: The manuscript reports the relationship between DCR and MI measures in humans.

claim: Macaques showed either high values of MI color or MI side, indicating coordination was not achieved by dynamic turn-taking.
source: In contrast to humans, monkeys showed either high values of MI color or MI side indicating that the resulting coordination was not achieved by dynamic turn-taking (Figure 2D).
evidence: The manuscript reports the MI patterns in macaques, and Figure 2D shows this data.

claim: Ten of 19 human pairs were close to the main diagonal in MI space, corresponding to similar values of MI side and MI color, denoting trial-by-trial or block-wise turn-taking.
source: Ten of 19 human pairs were close to the main diagonal, corresponding to similar values of MI side and MI color. These locations denote trial-by-trial or block-wise turn-taking – a signature of dynamic coordination.
evidence: The manuscript describes the MI pattern for turn-taking human pairs, and Figure 3 shows this data.

claim: Nine macaque pairs showed simple static side-based or single target color-based coordination, but did not employ dynamic coordination.
source: In contrast to humans, nine macaque pairs showed simple static side-based (four pairs) or single target color-based (five pairs) coordination, with different levels of coordination strength, but did not employ dynamic coordination.
evidence: The manuscript describes the coordination strategies in macaque pairs, and Figure 3 shows this data.

claim: All five macaque pairs coordinating on fixed color converged on the faster monkey's preferred color.
source: Remarkably, all five macaque pairs coordinating on the fixed color converged on the faster monkey's preferred color (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports the relationship between action time and color preference in macaque pairs.

claim: For static side coordination in macaques, all three pairs with significant action time differences converged on the faster monkey's less effortful side closer to the acting arm.
source: Likewise, for the static side coordination, all three (out of four) pairs where there was a significant difference in action times between the two agents converged on the faster monkey's less effortful side closer to the acting arm (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports the relationship between action time and side preference in macaque pairs.

claim: In non-turn-taking human dyads coordinating on fixed color, the faster agent led to its own color and the slower agent followed, or the faster agent led to the partner's color and the partner followed.
source: In humans, such static Leader-Follower relationship also transpired in non-turn-taking dyads coordinating on the fixed color (Supplementary file 1), where the faster agent led to its own color and the slower agent followed (e.g., pairs 10 and 14), or the faster agent led to the partner's color and the partner followed (e.g. pair 18).
evidence: The manuscript reports the Leader-Follower patterns in human pairs.

claim: Static coordination in macaques and some human dyads was shaped by the faster agent's preferences.
source: This implies that the static coordination in macaques and some human dyads was shaped by the faster agent's preferences.
evidence: The manuscript draws a conclusion from the observed action time patterns.

claim: Before confederate training, both monkeys adopted either a fixed side or fixed color strategy with macaque partners.
source: Before confederate training, both monkeys adopted either a fixed side or fixed color strategy with the macaque partners (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports the pre-training behavior of the two monkeys.

claim: When paired with the confederate, both monkeys started with a strong bias for selecting their own preferred color but over time changed to reliable coordination.
source: When paired with the confederate, both monkeys started with a strong bias for selecting their own preferred color but over time changed to reliable coordination (Figure 4A, B, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B for another monkey).
evidence: The manuscript reports the behavioral change during confederate training, and Figures 4A, B show this data.

claim: In later confederate training sessions, the animals reacted considerably slower in blocks where the confederate was selecting the animals' non-preferred color.
source: In later sessions, the animals reacted considerably slower in those blocks in which the confederate was selecting the animals' non-preferred color, as if waiting for the confederate to commit to an action.
evidence: The manuscript reports the action time pattern during confederate training.

claim: In confederate-trained macaques, there was a strong correlation between the modeled probability to see the partner's choice and the observed likelihood of following to the faster agent's color.
source: Figure 6A shows macaque agent A's probability to select his non-preferred color, the 'fraction of choosing other's' (the inverted fraction of choosing own) and the modeled probability for A to see B's choice before A made own choice, and the same for macaque agent B (see Materials and methods for details on modeling). In both monkeys, there was a strong correlation between the model and the observation, ranging from 0.92 for smoothed data to 0.64 for unsmoothed data, all significant at p<0.001.
evidence: The manuscript reports the correlation analysis with statistical significance, and Figure 6A shows this data.

claim: Strong positive correlations between action visibility and 'following' behavior were present in all six post-confederate-trained sessions.
source: Strong positive correlations between action visibility and 'following' behavior were present in all six post-confederate-trained sessions, indicating bouts of dynamic coordination (Figure 6—figure supplement 1; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports the consistency of correlations across sessions.

claim: Monkeys failed to coordinate when they could not see the confederate's actions due to an opaque barrier.
source: In both monkeys, the 'following' behavior ceased and they reverted to selecting their own preferred colors irrespective of the confederate's choices, who – by design – continued the block strategy (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The manuscript reports the effect of blocking action visibility, and Figures 4C show this data.

claim: There was a significant difference in monkey's action times when selecting the monkey's preferred and non-preferred color in the transparent condition, but no difference in the opaque condition.
source: In line with this observation, there was a significant difference in the monkey's action times when selecting the monkey's preferred (blue) and the non-preferred (red) color in the transparent condition, but no difference in the opaque condition.
evidence: The manuscript reports the action time analysis comparing transparent and opaque conditions.

claim: The immediate visual information about partner's actions and not merely monitoring reward history drove and maintained the macaques' 'following' behavior in transparent settings.
source: These results imply that the immediate visual information about partner's actions and not merely monitoring reward history drove and maintained the macaques' 'following' behavior in transparent settings.
evidence: The manuscript draws a conclusion from the opaque barrier experiment.

claim: After confederate training, the coordination behavior of the macaque pair changed noticeably.
source: The pair's coordination behavior changed noticeably after training with a confederate.
evidence: The manuscript reports the behavioral change after confederate training.

claim: In the second post-confederate session, the macaque pair repeatedly alternated between the two colors in long blocks.
source: The most interesting phase was during the second session, in which the animals repeatedly alternated between the two colors in long blocks (Figure 5B).
evidence: The manuscript reports the turn-taking behavior in the second session, and Figure 5B shows this data.

claim: After confederate training, the coordination strength increased and dynamic coordination resulted in turn-taking behavior in two sessions.
source: The mutual information measures as well as the DCR values indicate that after confederate training, the coordination strength increased and dynamic coordination resulted in turn-taking behavior in two sessions (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports the MI and DCR analysis after confederate training, and Figure 5D shows this data.

claim: In the session where macaques exhibited apparent turn-taking behavior, the faster animal selected the preferred color while the slower animal accommodated.
source: Indeed, in the session in which the animals exhibited apparent turn-taking behavior (Figure 5B), the faster animal (Leader) selected the preferred color, while the slower animal (Follower) had to accommodate.
evidence: The manuscript reports the Leader-Follower dynamics in the turn-taking session, and Figure 5B shows this data.

claim: The dynamic coordination in the confederate-trained macaque pair arose within a competitive interaction.
source: Thus, the dynamic coordination arose within a competitive interaction.
evidence: The manuscript draws a conclusion about the nature of macaque turn-taking.

claim: Human participants did not show a strong trial-by-trial relationship between relative action time differences and choices.
source: In contrast, human participants did not show a strong trial-by-trial relationship between relative action time differences and choices (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: The manuscript reports the lack of correlation in human pairs.

claim: In 47% of human pairs, the absolute difference in action times between agents significantly differed in coordinated trials compared to uncoordinated trials.
source: Indeed, in 47% (9 of 19) of human pairs, the absolute difference in action times between the agents significantly differed in coordinated trials compared to uncoordinated trials (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports the proportion of human pairs showing action time differences.

claim: Turn-taking human dyads had a larger absolute action time difference than non-turn-taking dyads.
source: Furthermore, turn-taking dyads had a larger absolute action time difference (102.7 ± 38.7 ms, N 10) than non-turn-taking dyads (61.3 ± 21.6 ms, N 9; t-test correcting for unequal variance t(14.4) 2.918; p=0.011); this difference was mostly driven by the coordinated trials (105.0 ± 41.5 ms, N 10 versus 64.7±24.1 ms, N 7; t(14.7) 2.523; p=0.024), while a similar trend in trials without coordination did not reach significance (93.8 ± 29.2 ms, N 10 versus 69.5 ± 39.7 ms, N 9; t(14.6) 1.512; p=0.152).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical comparison of action time differences between turn-taking and non-turn-taking human dyads.

claim: Turn-takers tended to pay more attention to partner's actions and wait more for each other during coordination.
source: This implies that turn-takers tended to pay more attention to partner's actions and wait more for each other during the coordination.
evidence: The manuscript draws a conclusion from the action time analysis.

claim: For confederate-trained macaques, the visibility of the other's action before making one's own decision correlated with the probability to follow the choice of the other.
source: The action time analyses show that for the confederate-trained macaques, the visibility of the other's action before making one's own decision correlated with the probability to follow the choice of the other, with the faster monkey 'selfishly' selecting its own preference.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the action time correlation findings in macaques.

claim: Turn-taking in humans did not rely on temporal competition.
source: Turn-taking in humans, however, did not rely on temporal competition.
evidence: The manuscript contrasts human and macaque turn-taking mechanisms.

claim: Macaques transitioned between periods of coordination using short periods of non-coordination, while turn-taking humans tended to switch seamlessly between the two coordination options.
source: Macaques transitioned between periods of coordination using short periods of non-coordination, while turn-taking humans tended to switch seamlessly between the two coordination options without verbal communication (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: The manuscript reports the difference in transition patterns between species.

claim: Turn-taking humans showed a high and roughly equal amount of benevolent and selfish seamless switches by a faster player.
source: Turn-taking humans showed a high and roughly equal amount of benevolent and selfish seamless switches by a faster player (Figure 7A, teal underlay).
evidence: The manuscript reports the switching behavior in turn-taking humans, and Figure 7A shows this data.

claim: Confederate-trained macaques and non-turn-taking humans showed only very few seamless switches.
source: Confederate-trained macaques and non-turn-taking humans showed only very few seamless switches.
evidence: The manuscript reports the low frequency of seamless switches in these groups.

claim: When turn-taking humans showed uncoordinated trials, they lay along the unity diagonal, indicating a benevolent intention to initiate the switch to the other's preferred color in half of these trials.
source: Alternative to seamless switches, agents can end the current coordination block by switching to non-coordination. These trials can be used to initiate or 'signal' a switch of coordination. When turn-taking humans showed uncoordinated trials they lay along the unity diagonal, indicating a benevolent intention to initiate the switch to the other's preferred color in half of these trials (Figure 7B).
evidence: The manuscript reports the pattern of uncoordinated trials in turn-taking humans, and Figure 7B shows this data.

claim: All macaque pairs were below the unity diagonal in uncoordinated trials, indicating a selfish preference for own color.
source: All macaque pairs were below the unity diagonal, indicating a selfish preference for own color.
evidence: The manuscript reports the pattern of uncoordinated trials in macaque pairs.

source: Liquid reward for monkeys was delivered via computer-controlled peristaltic fluid pumps, for every correctly performed trial.
evidence: The manuscript describes the reward delivery system for macaques.

claim: In the BoS implementation, agents chose between two differently colored targets placed on the left and right side of the display.

source: Each target color was associated with a higher reward for one of the agents resulting in individually preferred targets.

evidence: The manuscript describes the coordination bonus in the task.

claim: Targets were light blue circles of 35 mm diameter with either a red or yellow ring.
source: Targets were light blue circles of 35 mm diameter with either a red (individually-preferred target for agent A) or a yellow (individually-preferred target for agent B) rings (for better visualization, we replaced yellow and red rings with blue and red solid targets in the figures and the text).

source: Subjects had 1500 ms to touch this initial fixation target with the instructed hand.

source: After both subjects touched the fixation target they had to hold it for 500 ms.
evidence: The manuscript describes the fixation hold period.

claim: Two choice targets appeared at one of 3 different pairs of positions after the fixation hold period.
source: Then two choice targets appeared at 1 of 3 different pairs of positions (140 mm to the left and right of the central fixation target and either at the same height as the central fixation target or 35 mm below or 35 mm above it).
evidence: The manuscript describes the spatial arrangement of choice targets.

claim: The 'red' target location was randomized equally over all six positions, balanced in sets of 18 trials.
source: We randomized the 'red' location equally over all six positions, balanced in sets of 18 trials with each of the six 'red' positions appearing three times, and vertically mirrored the opposite location.
evidence: The manuscript describes the randomization procedure for target positions.

claim: Subjects had 1500 ms to make their choice and touch one of the targets.
source: Subjects had 1500 ms to make their choice and touch one of the targets.
evidence: The manuscript describes the timing constraint for target selection.

evidence: The manuscript describes the target hold period after selection.

claim: The amount of reward earned by each subject was signaled by two sequential series of auditory pulses with different pitch for each subject.
source: The amount of reward earned by each subject was signaled by two sequential series of auditory pulses (always first for the subject on side B then on side A), with a different pitch for each subject.
evidence: The manuscript describes the auditory reward feedback system.

claim: For macaques, liquid was delivered as reward (approximately 0.14 ml per pulse) concurrently with the auditory pulses.
source: For the monkeys, we delivered liquid as a reward (approximately 0.14 ml per pulse) concurrently with the auditory pulses directed towards the respective monkey's side; humans were instructed to expect 'a few' cents per pulse, and the accumulated earnings were paid out as a lump sum after the experiment.
evidence: The manuscript describes the reward delivery for macaques.

claim: Humans were instructed to expect 'a few' cents per pulse, and accumulated earnings were paid out as a lump sum after the experiment.
source: For the monkeys, we delivered liquid as a reward (approximately 0.14 ml per pulse) concurrently with the auditory pulses directed towards the respective monkey's side; humans were instructed to expect 'a few' cents per pulse, and the accumulated earnings were paid out as a lump sum after the experiment.
evidence: The manuscript describes the reward delivery for humans.

claim: After the reward period, subjects had to wait for an inter-trial interval of 1500 ms before they could initiate the next trial.
source: After the reward period, subjects had to wait for an inter-trial interval of 1500 ms before they could initiate the next trial.
evidence: The manuscript describes the inter-trial interval duration.

evidence: The manuscript describes the side randomization procedure.

evidence: The manuscript describes the solo training procedure for humans.

source: Subjects were instructed to use the right hand.
evidence: The manuscript describes the hand instruction for human subjects.

evidence: The manuscript describes the criterion for pairing macaques.

source: Thereafter, pairs of macaques worked together in the dyadic version of the task, for 11 ± 7 sessions (range 4–25).
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of dyadic sessions for macaque pairs.
